81.t: Jazz covers too much territory; ragtime
81.s: Johnson says jazz is pasted onto too much music and that he got nothing out of ragtime.
81.ch: Reel 3: defining jazz and the blues
81.q: Well, just like I said, it covers too much territory -- you can put jazz in too many spots, and it doesn't belong in those places. Jazz should have a special spot of its own. They got to throwing jazz around, and just pasted it on the wall everywhere. Jazz, jazz, jazz.

81.t: Jazz did not originate only in New Orleans
81.s: Jazz arose in many places, and Kansas City and New Orleans groups play the same blues differently.
81.ch: Reel 3: defining jazz and the blues
81.q: Yeah, well ... jazz originated all over the United States in certain spots. Didn't just -- jazz just wasn't born in New Orleans.

81.t: Jazz and the problem of calling everything jazz
81.s: Music has always been part of him but too much is called jazz.
81.ch: Porch interview and Jazz Train plans
81.q: Well, I'm trying -- I'm still trying. You know? Music has always been a part of me, I liked it and I enjoyed it, but the point of jazz, that's so hard to define -- jazz incorporates so much music. A lot of music that is not jazz is sometimes called jazz.

81.s: Johnson explains that jazz melded many kinds of music out of ragtime in the 1930s, and that he enjoyed swing as a listener.
81.ch: Porch interview and Jazz Train plans
81.q: Well, jazz comes in a multitude of music. Jazz -- they have made jazz now responsible for so much music, that it isn't jazz.

81.s: Johnson challenges Rasch to say what jazz is before he will say whether his music belongs in it.
81.ch: Telephone reels: blues and Bessie Smith
81.q: It was a song, because if I write a song and don't take that sound (inaudible) but if I write a muse jazz. Now, you're going to write some jazz, all right, I'll write some jazz.

22.t: Ragtime versus jazz in New Orleans before 1916
22.s: New Orleans bands played two-beat syncopated ragtime, not jazz, until about 1916.
22.q: Yes, it was called ragtime. Uh-huh. It had the syncopation to a four-beat music, but ours was syncopated to a march beat, or a two-beat.

22.t: Nine months in Chicago and the birth of jazz
22.s: In Chicago the band added syncopation to a one step, the crowd demanded jazz, and the name was added to the band.
22.q: Nine months. We were there nine months. It was in Chicago that I assumed we were going to be a flop, and I said to the boys, let me swing one of those things that we played in the carnival parades and put some syncopation to it. I see they're doing a one step here. I used to dance very well.

22.t: First hearing the word jazz in Chicago and Harry James
22.s: La Rocca says he first heard the word jazz in Chicago, that manager Harry James put it on the band, and that it had underworld associations.
22.ch: The word jazz and the band's New York success
22.q: Well, I never heard of the word jazz in New Orleans. I never knew what the word jazz meant. After I was in Chicago, about a week, a couple kept hollering, jazz it up, jazz it up, jazz it up.

22.t: Rust: ragtime bands versus jazz, and thanks
22.s: Rust argues Sousa, Pryor and others played written ragtime, while the ODJB were the first jazz recordings; he closes his statement.
22.q: it's easy enough to listen to them. I've only got to listen to those and compare them with the original Dixieland Jazz Band to realise that the one is Ragtime and the other is Jazz. The original Dixieland Jazz Band isn't called Jazz for Nothing. There are other musicians having laid claim to having…

639.t: Caller asks whether New Orleans or Memphis was the birthplace of jazz
639.s: A caller asks about New Orleans versus Memphis; Wiggs says New Orleans for jazz, Memphis for blues, though New Orleans had real blues too.
639.q: well history has it that New Orleans is a birthplace of jazz and Memphis is a birthplace of blues but uh uh uh we had uh the birth of the blues down here just as well as Memphis and I mean we got the real blues down here I love Memphis and I love the people in Memphis don't get me wrong uh but…

639.t: Caller and Wiggs on how jazz originated: field hands, minstrels, slaves and minuets
639.s: A caller credits work songs and minstrel parades; Wiggs gives his version of slaves imitating the madam's minuets and the African scale behind the blues.
639.q: Good morning, Joe. Mr. Wiggs, I enjoyed that last record of yours. I thought it was mighty fine. Thank you. How old are you, sir? I'm only 70. Only 70? I'm a stripling. Uh-huh. Well, Joe claims I'm over 100, so I... Oh, get away now. Outdate you. Not with that voice. Not with that voice. You're not…

639.t: Eddie Chance calls: jazz is only 55 years old and came out of Chicago
639.s: Eddie Chance, Tom Brown's nephew, argues about where jazz was named, praises Emmett Hardy and Red Bolman and says real jazz comes from the body.
639.q: baby. That will be coming up shortly, but we want to go back to the multi-phones with another call here for you. Good morning. You're on the air with Dick Allen of Tulane University. And Mr. Johnny Wiggs. Yes, sir. Go ahead. This is Eddie Jazz. One of the original jazz man. See, I like to set the…

639.t: How the word 'jazz' was attached to Tom Brown's band
639.s: Allen and Wiggs say the name was put on Tom Brown's band in Chicago to hurt it but it backfired; Chance makes peace.
639.q: Well, I tell you, the gentleman said so many things, I really wouldn't know where to start on.

418.t: What the music was called before jazz
418.s: He does not know where the word jazz came from; the music of the minstrel shows was called ragtime.
418.q: Yeah, Ragtime. I guess that was called Ragtime probably, you know.

418.s: Dickenson thinks the pieces called Dixieland were mostly marches jazzed up with syncopation into strutting music, different from ragtime.
418.q: That's just some numbers -- yeah, just some numbers that -- really, those pieces they call Dixieland usually -- well marches. They were usually marches.

418.s: Dickenson thinks the pieces called Dixieland were marches jazzed up with syncopation, different from ragtime.
418.q: I don't know. I don't know. I guess they called it a Dixieland band. So what's a band? A band is a band that... I guess they used it for marching bands, you know, and... But they jazzed it up a little. [SINGS REFRAIN "HURRAY FOR THE RED, WHITE AND BLUE" STRAIGHT TIME, THEN SYNCOPATED] You know,…

418.s: Dickenson thinks the pieces called Dixieland were marches jazzed up with syncopation, different from ragtime.
418.q: That's just some numbers -- yeah, just some numbers that -- really those pieces they call Dixieland usually -- well marches. They were usually marches.

648.t: Jelly Roll Morton, the word jazz and Armstrong and Oliver dates
648.s: Brown remembers hearing Morton in Chicago, offers a French derivation for the word jazz, and cites dates for Armstrong and Oliver.
648.ch: Origins of jazz and the district
648.q: I think this is something I... For some information, I took out of some of the books sometime. In fact, Jelly Roll, Jelly Roll Morton. Well, he happened to be in Chicago. Was, he was 20, and in Chicago in 1905. Born in 1885 in New Orleans. Found in 1941. I guess you got something with that fella,…

648.s: Brown says hot music began in New Orleans from plantation singing, riverfront roustabouts and church music.
648.q: More so down in New Orleans. It was all through the plantations and things like that. The old Negroes out there, I used to many times when I was a kid go along the river, and these Negro roasterabouts would be sitting out on a cotton bale waiting for the boats. And they'd be singing. And they'd…

648.t: Red-light district music was not early jazz
648.s: Brown rejects the writers' view that jazz came from the district; its barrelhouse, slow-drag music differed from his lively dance music.
648.ch: Origins of jazz and the district
648.q: To me, no, that's completely out. That's wrong. But the majority of writers, they could... But that's the easiest way to write about it, see? That everything came from the district. That's right, but it isn't. So the music down there was entirely different.

112.t: Ragtime and why his parents disapproved
112.s: He explains that ragtime used four-four time unlike European waltzes and one-steps, and that his parents thought only bums played it.
112.q: : Yes, there was only ragtime music and carnival music, that's all they used in those days. See, because we hadn't got up to the place, And, you see, the blacks were the first ones to use four-four. And have any ragtime at all.

112.s: Wooding discusses when he first heard the word jazz and how jazz and funk came to mean what they do.
112.q: Well, the first time that I ever heard of jazz was after we come back here, let's see -- well, in Atlantic City, we started playing it. Because I opened up with a -- I opened down there and then there were -- Ed Major who was with Charley Johnson -- they played quite a lot of jazz. They played jazz…

112.s: The band played Blue Danube but audiences wanted jazz, a word Wooding says had sexual undertones.
112.ch: Second European tour and the crash
112.q: We always played that. And the -- cause see, when we had been playing it like we do our work, but it's up fast, you know what I mean. And it has this ring to it. Strauss waltzes, we liked those and I played one or two of them. But not many because they wouldn't want us there for that. They wanted…

49.t: Smoke wagon slang and the first time he heard the word jazz
49.s: He defines 'smoke wagon' and says ragtime gave way to the word jazz that he cannot trace.
49.q: Yeah, pistol. That's what you call a pistol? Yeah, big long things. What they used to do, it used to be, the police used to carry it mostly. It was a .38. It was built on a .41 frame. So it was, it had about a seven, eight inch barrel, you see. And the thing was big long to stick it down in here…

49.t: The Fisher card and Red Long's New Orleans Swing Band
49.s: He says the word jazz was on Fisher's 1911 card and that he played in Red Long's New Orleans Swing Band at the Ritz decades before Goodman.
49.q: No, no. If I said so, I'd be lying, Dick. I don't. This all of a sudden there it was. But even before, you know, I was a kid. But even before, I can go back this far, but even before they ever had jazz bands at all, ragtime bands or whatever you want to call them. You see, like I tell you, I had a…

843.t: Bill Russell on the word jazz, its New Orleans origin and reading music
843.s: Russell says the name jazz came in Chicago, older musicians said ragtime, the music started in New Orleans, and many early players read music.
843.q: No, that's another thing a lot of people have been talking and arguing about for years. Actually, it seems the name jazz has applied to the music, wasn't used with the music until it got to Chicago, probably, as far as we know. Although sometimes you'll find people down here that'll claim they…

843.t: Jazz as American, with the best bands from New Orleans
843.s: Russell argues that jazz developed in America and that most of the better bands originated in New Orleans.
843.q: Oh yes, it seemed to be something definitely developed in America, and I'm ready to believe from what I've seen and heard, that most of the better bands did originate here. Right in New Orleans. Right in New Orleans. There's been just entirely too many musicians here to say that, well, it's…

195.t: Final summary: Dallas blues and Texas as a birthplace of jazz
195.s: Parker says the Doughboys differed from eastern bands through kinship with Dallas blues, Lead Belly and Blind Lemon and closeness to the Gulf. He calls Texas a separate birthplace of jazz.
195.q: well is anything there that you want about an hour and a half but is there anything there that you really want oh yeah you might think of the last question oh now Ed a last minute summary now one of the differences that makes what the music I've been talking about the Doe Boys and the Fort Worth…

195.t: Texas and Mexican influence on New Orleans jazz
195.s: He argues the western influence came up from Mexico through Texas to New Orleans and claims Texas jazz is underrated. Crawford notes Texas jazz towns, and Parker recalls playing a summer in New Orleans.
195.q: composite area blues now yes it has its roots in all these uh-huh sure sure sure anytime you hear even anytime minstrel or circus bands and all the old roots of the blues will tie them all with the whole American theme comment now we didn't say anything about minstrel bands or circus bands I'm not…

1.t: Scott Joplin and ragtime compared with Armstrong
1.s: Asked about Joplin, Barker says ragtime is trained, classical piano tied to dances, and Armstrong is not ragtime.
1.q: Louie's stomp down. Louie's, Joplin is a classical thing taken from Chopin, some things that Chopin has done, that type of two-handed piano. Technical, trained piano. That is Joplin. That's ragtime.

1.t: Jelly Roll's stomps and his claim to have invented jazz
1.s: Danny explains that Jelly Roll slowed ragtime into stomps and thought his music the only real jazz, hating the fast tempos of Chick Webb.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Well, Jelly Roll, you know, played stomp. He slowed down rag, and he called it stomps -- stomp-down. You see, everybody, Eubie Blake, everybody...Joe Jordan... All them people was playing Scott Joplin's legitimate thing. Jelly Roll took it and slowed it down. [SINGS A REFRAIN] It's probably because…

23.t: Why jazz must be defined; the Modern Jazz Quartet
23.s: Rose argues critics never define jazz, so the word means nothing. He says the MJQ derives from European chamber music, not jazz.
23.q: Oh, certainly. Actually, all cultural forms about which experts write usually, invariably, have a fundamental set of criteria which are necessary in order for people to be able to deal with them intelligently. Now, most important is this, and that is that when any critic or expert discusses any…

23.t: Jazz as a product of place, not race; blues is separate
23.s: Rose says jazz came from New Orleans, not from blacks coming north, and that the blues was not fundamental to it. He says New Orleans was a happy town hostile to the blues, and old labels show blues and jazz as separate forms.
23.q: In the first place, in the first place, your general pursuit of this matter reflects certain glaring prejudices, which it is necessary to deal with because they are not exclusively yours. And that is mostly marked by your discussion based on the black man coming north, you see, which is, as far as…

887.t: African, Haitian and Caribbean roots of the beat
887.s: Cahn sees Indian music as a base for New Orleans music, via Africa, Haiti and Santo Domingo; a Paul Oliver Africa field recording is played.
887.q: I think it's, it takes its base or is the base for a lot of New Orleans music. You'll find that the beat is very similar. It comes possibly from Africa through Santa Domingo and Haiti up, up to New Orleans. And there's no question in my mind that it was part of the slave music back in the 1850s or…

887.t: New Orleans music as a unique blend
887.s: Cahn says jazz could only come from New Orleans, blending French martial music, Congo Square, riverfront labor and street vendors.
887.q: Yes, I've had to influence quite a bit of New Orleans music, but New Orleans music is just a real go-around. It's influenced by many, many things and influences many, many things. It seems to be just, as it has been said, these things could only happen in New Orleans because of the music. No other…

1048.t: Defining terms and genres: classic rag, folk rag, Bob Milne
1048.s: Johnson says categories must be defined and respected; she explains classic versus folk ragtime and improvisation, citing Bob Milne, and infighting within genres.
1048.q: You have to define it and you have to respect the various genres too. That’s the other part of it. I think I agree with Mat when he says it’s all good music. But you don’t sell it based on it’s all good music. In the same, Wycliffe saying can’t it all be considered jazz, but it really can’t because…

1048.s: Johnson discusses why she prefers 'traditional jazz', how Dixieland became associated with novelty and ice cream social music, and Wild Bill Davison's dislike of it.
1048.q: Well trad jazz — it’s fine. You know it’s just a shortcut. And there’s nothing wrong with that except some people think of it as being British. I don’t.

547.t: Origins of batá rhythms in Yorubaland and Cuba
547.s: Rowe asks how rhythms connect to deities; Rendón says batá comes from Nigeria, evolved in Cuba from the early 1800s.
547.q: That’s a good question because the music, the batá music that we played for you yesterday, it’s — the origins is from Nigeria, Yorubaland. And if you listen to, I’ve listened to the batá drumming that’s still in existence there and a lot of it doesn’t sound like what has evolved in Cuba and the…

547.s: The Latin tinge, the cinquillo rhythm, Mexican teachers in New Orleans, and Gottschalk.
547.q: There was a lot of, I’m sure you have that book, “The Latin Tinge” who was the author of that? I don’t remember but you know what I’m talking about.

142.t: Cuban officials, dual repertoire and defining jazz
142.s: Irakere kept separate concert and dance repertoires, with the jazz spirit in both; when Americans labelled it jazz, officials said it was too late.
142.q: They have nothing to do, and the thing is that Irakere was the first band, no the only band in the world, that I know—at least in Cuba the only band that I know—that have two totally different repertoire, totally different. We had, we decide on purpose a concert repertoire as well as a dance…

142.t: Mario Bauza on who plays true Latin jazz
142.s: He explains using Latin American elements in jazz, and Bauza's remark that he was the only one doing Latin jazz while others did Afro-Cuban jazz.
142.q: Always I have the inclination to use elements of Latin America, and the best vehicle to do that is Jazz music. It is the music of the immigrants, is a multi-national culture, but talking about Latin Jazz, for example, Mario Bauza is once he say an exaggeration, but I am going to mention it now.…

507.t: How ragtime turned into jazz, and Treemonisha's message
507.s: He describes ragtime's slow transformation into jazz and the themes of Joplin's opera.
507.q: then in the early ’20s, did musicians come along who really could improvise, Bix [Beiderbecke] being one of them, and of course Louis Armstrong being one of them. But mostly what at first happened – I know this from first-hand, of old-timers that I talked to 40 years ago, who had played in 1908 and…

507.s: He explains how the name arose and gained fame after a John Wilson headline.
507.q: I will. I will. But this is important, because the reason I got into that – because this whole movement of identifying with jazz, both by American composers like Louis Gruenberg and of course [George] Gershwin to some extent, too, and the European composers in Poland, in Germany, in Italy,…

382.t: What jazz means, and swing versus jazz
382.s: She discusses being called a jazz singer, that swing replaced jazz, ragtime versus jazz, and the 'jazz' label Duke Ellington disliked.
382.q: Someone was saying, how did I feel about being called a jazz singer because I wasn't called a jazz singer in the beginning. Of course, my answer to that is that in 1937 jazz, you know, as an expression was considered passe and I actually came in on the swing era, so I guess --

382.t: Scat and her first jazz record
382.s: She never went into scat; the Bob Wilber album was her first jazz record, in her own view, the earlier albums were balladeer work.
382.ch: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
382.q: I've never gone into the scat business, you know, I mean I can play around with a melody but I don't like the scat lyrics so to speak. I just like to play around with the melody and the harmony and the progressions.

91.t: Swing origins matter less than music that moves you
91.s: Carter finds origin questions unimportant: a technically dazzling player did not move him, and Jelly Roll claimed to invent jazz.
91.ch: The Savoy band and the Swing era
91.q: All right. For me, it isn't, you know. I don't think these terms have any particular significance. If the music is good and it moves you, fine, you know. Like I had a friend who took me to hear a musician a couple weeks ago back in California that he thought was fantastic. Of course, this man was…

91.t: The term swing and Hugues Panassie in Paris
91.s: He recalls swing becoming a public term during his 1935 European stay and discusses it with Panassie.
91.ch: The Savoy band and the Swing era
91.q: Yes, it was. As a matter of fact, I even remember now that when I went to Paris in 1935, I had a conversation about that with Hugues Panassie. And I think he used some French term for 'swing' that I think was -- my French is pretty bad at this point, but it seems it was Espes de la Banceloin.…

234.t: What is jazz? The word as a museum term
234.s: Gil declines to define jazz and says the word will become historical like other labels.
234.ch: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
234.q: I wouldn't want to describe jazz verbally any more then to just to play all the records that have been made by people, of music that isn't that isn't of the past and rhythmically it's not of the past.

234.t: The origin of the word jazz and what remains of it
234.s: Gil says jazz originally meant pelvic action, then discusses what is left of jazz and when to use the word. A Bambi aside interrupts.
234.ch: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
234.q: Jazz, the word jazz, originally before I ever heard the word jazz applied to music meant, pelvic action. Like you're jazzing. Jazzing, meaning you jazz. So it meant a pelvic motion so......

96.t: His father's attitude to jazz and ragtime
96.s: His father liked jazz but was in ragtime, which the boys found corny and jerky.
96.ch: Chicago boyhood and the Austin High Gang
96.q: Yes. Because, I don't know, it has to flow, it had to flow you know and it was a little too jerky for us in those days. We liked King Oliver and Louis Armstrong and the Wolverines. We started, Bix Beiderbecke and those guys.

96.s: He says ragtime did not allow improvisation and was corny to him, while gospel and spirituals were the root.
96.q: No, no. Absolutely not. It was sort of a, I don't know, the 'Twelfth Street Rag,' that's a rag. You could improvise actually on it now, but the people want to hear that, da, da, da, da, (IMITATES RAG)................ which is, doesn't fit in with my musical taste (I assure you) as jazz. But we used…

31.t: What jazz really is: tempo, not music
31.s: Whaley argues that jazz is tempo and swing, tells how 'jazz it up' became a word, and contrasts it with Paul Whiteman's sweet music.
31.ch: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
31.q: Music, jazz is not music. Jazz is tempo, see, years ago when Paul Whiteman was the king of syncopation, he used (sings) to play all that sweet music, see, 'Whispering' and 'I Love You,' see all that sweet music and that sophisticated swing, that's what it was. Paul Whiteman, he was the king of it.…

31.t: The word jazz, funky and eight measures
31.s: Whaley says Duke disliked the word jazz, and he and Hinton talk about how words like funky changed meaning.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: Well, you see, Duke, he didn't like that word jazz either, see, he cut it out. There ain't no jazz -- I used to tell people, it ain't jazz, it's tempo. Jazz this thing up,mess the music up. That's what they do, mess it up. You would never know the melody.

237.t: Lovett, Goodwin and Smith debate soul
237.s: Lovett says soul needs no reading, as in Louisiana work crews; Goodwin and Smith agree it comes from inside the player.
237.q: Well, you just don't have to read to play soul music I can tell you that, because down my way in Louisiana, you can take five or six guys just get together and put them off a truck working somewhere or anything man and they get together and you hear some of the best music you've ever heard in your…

237.t: What soul means and Smith's objection to 'soul music'
237.s: Goodwin says soul is playing what you feel; Smith complains of audiences asking for soul music after a set full of it.
237.q: Sure, and I think this is the best thing for a fellow. You know, this brings us down to what we call soul. This is a guy playing what he feels. This is a person playing what he feels. This is where the word soul comes from because he is playing himself. He is playing what we call soul.

173.s: Nobody played ragtime in his day; Nunez, who played by ear, joined the police band and is called the foundation of jazz. He says he played the written melody and violinists learned from him.
173.q: No, no. In our time, they never played that. The only man, like I told you before, that I heard putting the police band, got this fellow, Yellow Nunez, and I tell you, he couldn't read nothing, but he could, the minute he'd hear a piece, he could play it as good as you, you would notice. He had a…

771.t: Old-time music versus the origins of jazz
771.s: His father's generation played quadrilles, waltzes and dance books, not jazz; he credits Bolden and untrained routine players with starting jazz amid fast city life.
771.q: Well, they played at old time. You see, those days they had music that mostly looked like manuscript, but they called it German music, you know. They used to come from the old country, you know. Mm-hmm. And that's what they played. And they had a set of books they called Manhattan books, dance…

957.t: What jazz is: no writing, a gang of mistakes with a quick cover
957.s: Foster says jazz is whatever you make it, comes from the head, and is a run of mistakes covered quickly.
957.ch: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
957.q: You see, in the line, that's what I tell plenty of people, to my estimation, the jazz, there's no such thing about jazz. Jazz is what you make it. Uh-huh. See, because there's no writing for jazz. There's no music for jazz. Jazz comes out your head. Uh-huh. You never know what you're going to do…

920.t: Leaving New Orleans for Chicago and the Schiller Cafe; origin of 'jazz'
920.s: The band travels to Chicago in March 1916, opens at the Schiller Cafe, and a patron's shout gives them the name jazz band.
920.ch: Original Dixieland Jazz Band: Chicago and New York
920.q: Here we go. It's ready. We left New Orleans for Chicago Thursday, March 2, 1916, 8.30 a.m. I arrived in Chicago Friday, March 3, 1916, about 9.30. This train was late due to a severe snowstorm. Mom said, take you overboard. Mom don't know. We couldn't be bothered with those things besides it was…

479.t: Where the word jazz came from
479.s: He credits Nick LaRocca's band and the dance and spelling of 'jazz' in Chicago for the name.
479.q: The original Dixieland jazz band, he can vouch for it is Nick LaRocca on, Jack and Abbey. He don't like to talk to nobody about nothing the way I understand. They went up there and they had a dance called a shimmy. And dancing around the Shilla Cafe, they used to call it ass dance, jazz. They…

769.s: Jazz is conversation music played the authentic way, not arrangements, and he will keep that beat now Lewis has died.
769.q: I think there's quite a few years. Yeah, it's quite a few years. But I, now if, if they may call, call it jazz. You know, jazz is not a music of arrangements. You know, you don't play arrangements in jazz. Because that ain't the way it starts, that's not the authentic type. But you take a lot of…

871.s: They discuss two-beat versus four-beat playing, what Dixieland and ragtime meant, and why today's bands are not playing real Dixieland.
871.q: Then they'll double. It's like you're talking about. It's like I'm talking about. Well, that's the way the orchestra used to play. But they don't play like that now. And they didn't play nothing. I didn't know that guy definitely swing all together than what these guys had years ago. They were…

33.s: DeDroit says his first band was called a Jass band, a name Mr. Grunewald used.
33.ch: Radio, theaters and early dance forms
33.q: Exactly. My first band was called a Jazz Sass band. They didn't call it jazz, it was called Jazz Sass. J-A-S-S, if you want to look through here you'll find it, S-A-S-S. And we called it jazz. Mr. Grunwald called it the Jazz Sass band. And that was the name it was called, Jazz Sass.

624.t: Who originated jazz: Roppolo, Brunies, Stephens, Mares and Chink vs ragtime
624.s: Brunies rejects claims by others and says the New Orleans Rhythm Kings players originated jazz, while LaRocca's band played ragtime.
624.q: That's ridiculous. I'll tell you who originated jazz. It was Georgia Burns, Leo Rapola, Rag Baby Stevens, and Chink. Yeah, I believe it was Chink, Chink, Chink. And I don't know who was the other two. There were two more in the band. And them's the one who originated jazz. Some of the New Orleans…

431.t: Why jazz began in New Orleans: dancing, race and street parades
431.s: Kmen argues New Orleans' dance mania, Black dance musicians and parade bands produced jazz.
431.q: Well, this will have to be very general. But, uh, anybody who wants to support the generalities, but particulars, will be able to find evidences here in the written material, at least some of the stuff I've done. Uh, one thing that I believe is easily proved is that New Orleans was a unique city in…

763.t: First white jazz band he heard: the High Rollers
763.s: He recalls hearing the High Rollers, a white ragtime band, around 1908; the word jazz was then a bad word.
763.q: Well, now I can tell you about, let's see, 1905. No, I would say from about 1908 or something like that. Because what do I remember, I couldn't be no more than about nine or ten years old at the time. When I heard the first, when I heard the first jazz band, white jazz band, and that was the High…

271.t: The first string band with a horn; ragtime and jazz
